newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S. surgeon packs for Moscow as Yeltsin op nears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. surgeon packs for Moscow as Yeltsin op nears.

text.p: Doctors are in the final stages of preparing Boris Yeltsin for his heart operation and the Russian leader could go under the knife as early as next week.

As the president made some final administrative changes before heading for the operating table, top U.S. surgeon Michael DeBakey was packing his bags to fly to Moscow to determine whether Yeltsin was ready for bypass surgery.
Late on Tuesday the Kremlin issued the first of what it said would be a regular series of health bulletins on the president, who is resting at a sanatorium outside Moscow.
"The main aim of the final stage of the preparation is to bring the patient to the peak of his current physical and physiological capabilities," the bulletin said.
All Yeltsin's meetings have been cancelled to allow for final preparations for the operation, it said.

DeBakey, the 88-year-old pioneer of bypass surgery, told Reuters that Yeltsin's operation, intended to improve blood flow to his heart, might be performed as early as next week. A firm date has not yet been fixed, he added.

"We're shooting for next week," said DeBakey, who will act as a consultant during the operation. He said he was making flight reservations and changing his schedule in preparation for his trip to Russia later this week.

Asked if Yeltsin was now considered strong enough for the surgery, DeBakey, speaking from his home base in Houston, Texas, said: "I hope so. I can't say definitely until I get there. That's one of the reasons I'm going to check on all that."
Yeltsin, 65, had two heart attacks last year and is believed to have suffered a third before his re-election in July for a second four-year term at the helm of the world's largest country.

The surgery is to be performed by Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who trained under DeBakey. Akchurin visited Houston recently to familiarise himself with equipment that DeBakey said has now been sent to Moscow.
DeBakey told CNN that, following his visit to Moscow in late September, Yeltsin's medical team set a six-week window for the surgery, contingent on improvements in his health.
"It's now believed that most of the things (health problems) are corrected, that his condition has improved and probably he will be ready this coming week," DeBakey said.
DeBakey said that Yeltsin would need a multiple bypass operation because of clogging in the arteries to his heart.
On Tuesday Yeltsin pressed on with changes in Russia's powerful Security Council following his sacking of the outspoken ex-soldier Alexander Lebed for insubordination.
Itar-Tass news agency said Yeltsin had appointed businessman Boris Berezovsky and military commander Leonid Mayorov as deputies to Ivan Rybkin, Lebed's successor as council secretary.

The Security Council, headed by Yeltsin, groups senior government ministers, including those of defence and the interior, and officials of the Federal Security Service (FSB), successor organisation of the Soviet-era KGB.
Yeltsin has been keen to restore stability in the organs of state after weeks of public squabbling among members of his entourage trying to increase their influence during his illness.

Lebed, a popular reserve general with his sights trained on the presidency, had upset the establishment with his off-the-cuff and often controversial remarks and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused him of planning a coup.
Yeltsin has also signalled to leaders of 89 Russian regions that he will not brook attempts by them to wrest more power from Moscow during his absence from active political life.
The president wants to meet the regional bosses and to make clear the Kremlin will try to cancel any local decision which does not coincide with its policy, Interfax news agency said.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, seen as a reliable pair of hands, has been given extra powers and will formally take the helm during Yeltsin's operation,
